Tides happen because the Moon's gravity pulls on the Earth, and it doesn't pull on every part of the planet equally. The side of the Earth facing the Moon is closer to it, so the Moon's gravitational pull there is stronger than it is on the Earth's center, while the far side of the Earth experiences a weaker pull. This difference in gravitational strength stretches the planet slightly, and because water is fluid and moves more easily than solid rock, the oceans respond most visibly. The result is that water bulges outward on the side of the Earth nearest the Moon, where the pull is strongest, and also on the opposite side, where the Moon's pull is weakest and the water is effectively left behind, bulging away from the Moon.

As the Earth rotates through these bulges each day, most coastal locations pass through two high tides and two low tides roughly every twenty-four hours and fifty minutes. The extra fifty minutes comes from the fact that the Moon is also moving in its orbit while the Earth spins, so the Earth has to rotate a little further before a given spot lines up with the Moon again.

The Sun plays a role too. Although it is vastly farther away, its enormous mass means its gravitational pull on the Earth is significant. When the Sun, Moon, and Earth line up during new and full moons, their tidal effects combine to produce spring tides, the highest of the month. When the Sun and Moon pull at right angles to each other, during the Moon's quarter phases, their effects partially cancel, producing weaker neap tides.

Local geography shapes the details. Coastline shape, ocean depth, and the shape of bays can amplify or dampen the tidal range, which is why some places barely notice the tide while others, like the Bay of Fundy, see water levels rise and fall by many meters.
